author: Law360 Pulse

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: The supplied excerpts contain only general publication disclaimers and licensing restrictions. They provide no substantive findings or arguments about multidisciplinary implementation, verification, task-specific evaluation, service redesign or lawyer replacement, so the source’s position relative to the cluster cannot be determined.

st.t: AI adoption: Enthusiasm cannot establish investment value
st.an: The survey supports the cluster’s bounded implementation account: adoption is rising but remains selective, frequent use correlates with perceived ease and optimism without establishing objective investment value, and firm training and resources are uneven. Persistent reliability, confidentiality and junior-development concerns further undercut any inference that enthusiasm alone demonstrates readiness or value.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The survey aligns closely with the cluster: lawyers report benefits concentrated in bounded tasks such as research, summarisation and correspondence, while identifying reliability, ethics, malpractice and loss of junior developmental work as major risks. Its findings are descriptive perceptions and expectations rather than evidence of autonomous practice, realised productivity or employment displacement.

kp.k: Survey documents U.S. law-firm lawyers’ reported AI experiences
kp.d: Law360 Pulse’s second annual AI Survey surveyed 390 lawyers from Nov. 6, 2024, to Jan. 13, 2025. Respondents were 28% associates, 25% equity partners, 9% nonequity partners, and 37% other roles, including staff attorneys, of counsel and solo practitioners. The findings concern reported usage, attitudes and firm practices; anticipated effects are respondents’ expectations rather than demonstrated outcomes.
qs: Law360 Pulse conducted the survey from Nov. 6, 2024, to Jan. 13, 2025.
Percentages may not add up to 100% due to rounding or the ability of participants to select multiple responses.
Participation was anonymous — unless anonymity was expressly waived.

kp.k: Reported adoption increased, concentrated in research and document tasks
kp.d: The substantive usage section reports adoption for at least one purpose rising from 35% in the 2024 survey to 54% in 2025. Across all respondents, current uses included legal research (40%), document summary (32%), correspondence (28%), document creation (27%), e-discovery or technology-assisted review (22%), and contract review and analysis (21%). The report says usage varied little by firm size or job title; men generally reported higher usage than women, and respondents under 60 somewhat higher usage than older respondents.

kp.k: Adoption intentions remain selective across legal tasks
kp.d: More than 20% reported plans for future use in nearly every surveyed use case except patent drafting. Nevertheless, 55% had no plans to use generative AI for contract review and analysis, 70% for billing, 71% for compliance, 72% for client intake and 85% for patent drafting. Even among intellectual property lawyers, 57% resisted using it for patent drafting. These are stated intentions, not forecasts of actual adoption.

kp.k: Frequent users apply AI across more tasks
kp.d: Across the full sample, 27% reported using AI at least three times weekly, approximately another quarter used it less frequently, and 48% did not currently use it or reported never using it. Frequent users reported legal research use at 82%, document summary at 78%, correspondence at 73% and document creation at 71%; corresponding infrequent-user figures were 64%, 40%, 34% and 33%. The report notes an inconsistency among current users: 4% subsequently said they never used generative AI at work.

kp.k: Reported benefits and positive sentiment track usage frequency
kp.d: Among current users, 77% said AI made work easier, 16% reported no effect and 6% said it made work harder. Work became easier for 94% of frequent users versus 66% of infrequent users. Across the full sample, 35% expressed positive sentiment toward industry adoption, 34% neutral sentiment and 26% negative sentiment. Frequent users were 73% positive, while nonusers were 11% positive and 44% negative. These comparisons document associations between usage and attitudes.
qs: Which of the following best captures your sentiment toward AI adoption in the legal industry?
Positive: The changes are likely to beneﬁt legal practice overall
Neutral: Both the pros and cons are sizable
Negative: The changes are likely to damage legal practice overall

kp.k: Efficiency, client savings and expanded service are anticipated benefits
kp.d: Respondents envisioned increased administrative efficiency (69%), cost savings passed to clients (41%), expanded caseloads through streamlined work (36%), and expanded service to low-income clients (20%). Frequent users anticipated these benefits more often, at 86%, 63%, 62% and 38%, respectively. The introduction describes competitive pressure to adopt AI to pass savings to clients or increase profits; the survey does not present these expected effects as measured financial or access-to-justice outcomes.
qs: Which of the following do you envision as positive effects of law firms’ adoption of generative AI?
Expanded service to low-income clients
Ability to expand caseload due to streamlined work
Cost savings being passed along to clients

kp.k: Reliability, malpractice, ethics and confidentiality dominate concerns
kp.d: As anticipated negative effects, 82% selected incorrect AI responses and 82% selected AI learning inaccurate information and passing it on; 62% selected potential malpractice claims. Separately, 79% were concerned about AI’s imperfect grasp of legal ethics and standards, 62% about confidentiality, security and privacy, and 55% each about institutional knowledge loss and keeping pace with technological advances. These percentages measure concerns, not model error rates or observed malpractice incidents.
qs: Which of the following do you envision as negative effects of law firms’ adoption of generative AI?
AI learning inaccurate information and passing it on
Potential malpractice claims for AI usage
AI’s imperfect grasp of legal ethics and standards
Difficulty in maintaining client confidentiality, security and data privacy

kp.k: Junior lawyers express stronger billing and employment anxieties
kp.d: Overall, 52% anticipated fewer opportunities for new lawyers to perform basic legal work, 25% fewer billable hours and 24% loss of white-collar jobs. Associates more often selected fewer billable hours than partners (38% versus 19%) and job losses (34% versus 13%). Women more often anticipated fewer basic-work opportunities for new lawyers than men (64% versus 49%). Reduced billable hours concerned 43% at midsize firms, compared with 20% at smaller firms and 33% at the largest firms. These are perceived risks, not demonstrated staffing reductions.

Fewer billable hours

kp.k: AI familiarity is expected to become professionally important
kp.d: The narrative reports that 72% considered AI familiarity important or very important for lawyers over the next five years, including 95% of frequent users, 85% of infrequent users and 52% of nonusers. Cost concerns also differed by resources: 41% at small firms, 37% at midsize firms and 31% at the largest firms were concerned about AI product costs.
qs: How important do you think it will be for lawyers to become more familiar with AI tools in the next five years?
Cost of AI products

kp.k: Firm guidance and training vary sharply by size
kp.d: Overall, 57% reported some firm guidance, 29% warnings against unauthorized use, 25% encouragement and 24% training offerings. Among frequent users, 51% reported encouragement and 40% training offerings. Training was offered according to 70% of respondents at firms with more than 600 attorneys, 34% at firms with 101–600 attorneys and 13% at firms with 100 or fewer. The report suggests encouragement and training may influence adoption. The chart’s 'None of these apply' response was selected by 4%, 26% and 57%, respectively.

kp.k: Small-firm lawyers rely more on external AI training
kp.d: Overall, 12% received training from their firm alone, 13% from both their firm and another source, 29% only from another source, and 45% received none. At firms with more than 600 attorneys, 34% received firm-only training and 32% combined training; at firms with 100 or fewer, those figures were 5% and 9%. External-only training was reported by 36% at small firms versus 13% at large firms. The report interprets this disparity as placing a greater burden on small-firm lawyers to seek training themselves.

kp.k: AI-focused hiring is concentrated in the largest firms
kp.d: Across all respondents, 69% said their firm had neither hired nor was hiring for AI-specific roles; 7% reported an executive hire, 6% multiple hires, 2% active searches and 16% did not know. At the largest firms, 44% reported executive or multiple-person hiring, comprising 20% and 24%, respectively, while 43% did not know. At midsize and small firms, 55% and 85% reported no hiring or search. These figures describe lawyers’ knowledge of firm hiring rather than a census of positions.

kp.k: Larger firms invest more in tools and providers
kp.d: Internal generative AI development was reported by 15% overall, including 41% at firms with more than 600 attorneys, 18% at midsize firms and 9% at small firms. At the largest firms, another 43% were unsure about internal development. External-provider contracts were reported by 40% overall, with 70% at the largest firms, 41% at midsize firms and 33% at small firms; 57% at small firms reported no contract.

kp.k: ChatGPT leads reported tool use in fragmented market
kp.d: Among respondents answering the non-e-discovery tools question, 62% selected ChatGPT, 28% Lexis+ AI, 24% Microsoft Copilot, 20% Google Gemini, 17% Thomson Reuters CoCounsel, 6% Claude.ai and 5% each Harvey AI and Perplexity. The questionnaire allowed up to five choices. Reported e-discovery choices included Relativity aIR (29%), Everlaw AI Assistant (17%), DISCO Cecilia (16%), Epiq Discovery (13%) and Nextpoint (11%), with up to three choices allowed. The report characterizes legal-specific generative AI as fragmented and raises possible future consolidation. It discloses Law360’s ownership connection to Lexis+ AI’s developer.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Law360 Pulse reports expanding adoption and perceived benefits, alongside anticipated professional risks, unequal organisational support and a fragmented tools market.
pts.d: In its March 2025 report, with an introduction by Xavier Chauvris and Jack Collens, Law360 Pulse reports that generative AI use for at least one work purpose rose from 35% in its 2024 survey to 54% in the current survey. Legal research leads current applications at 40% of respondents, followed by document summary (32%), correspondence (28%) and document creation (27%). Frequent users employ AI across more tasks. Among current users, 77% say AI makes work easier, including 94% of frequent users and 66% of infrequent users. These are reported experiences rather than measured productivity gains. Respondents anticipate increased administrative efficiency (69%), savings passed to clients (41%), expanded caseloads (36%) and expanded services to low-income clients (20%). The introduction also describes competitive pressure to adopt AI to benefit clients or increase profits. Anticipated negative effects include incorrect responses and transmission of inaccurate information (82% each), malpractice claims (62%), reduced opportunities for new lawyers to perform basic work (52%), use without client choice or consent (41%), frivolous AI-generated litigation (38%), fewer billable hours (25%) and white-collar job losses (24%). Broader concerns include legal ethics (79%), confidentiality/security/privacy (62%), institutional knowledge loss (55%) and keeping pace with technology (55%). The report says 72% expect familiarity with AI tools to be important or very important within five years. It associates firm encouragement and training with greater adoption, and describes larger firms as better positioned to provide training, hire AI personnel, contract with providers and develop tools. It characterises legal-specific generative AI as fragmented and suggests possible future consolidation.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal evidence is an anonymous survey of 390 lawyers, including self-reported use, experiences, expectations and firm practices; market consolidation is an editorial possibility rather than a demonstrated outcome.
pts.d: Law360 Pulse surveyed lawyers at U.S. firms from November 6, 2024, to January 13, 2025. Participants included associates (28%), equity partners (25%), nonequity partners (9%) and other lawyer roles (37%). Respondents were 63% male, 29% female and 2% nonbinary, with 6% declining to state gender; 62% were under 60 and 35% were 60 or older. The report compares current adoption with its previous annual survey, but does not supply a matched longitudinal sample, sampling frame, response rate, weighting or uncertainty estimates. Its introduction describes previous use as less than one-third, whereas the detailed adoption section gives 35%; the latter is the explicit numerical comparison used here. Benefits and risks are survey answers, not independently measured savings, productivity, error rates, malpractice incidents or employment changes. The association between frequent use and favourable experiences does not establish whether use causes favourable views. Similarly, the training/adoption relationship is presented tentatively. Reported organisational differences include training offered by 70% of the largest-firm respondents' firms versus 13% of small-firm respondents' firms; internal tool development at 41% versus 9%; and provider contracts at 70% versus 33%. These are respondent reports, not a census of unique firms. Among those answering the external-tools question, ChatGPT was selected by 62%, Lexis+ AI by 28%, Microsoft Copilot by 24%, Gemini by 20%, CoCounsel by 17% and Harvey AI by 5%. These selections support the report's account of tool use but are not revenue-based market shares. The report discloses Law360's ownership by LexisNexis, which developed Lexis+ AI. No separate evidence is offered for future consolidation.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Current-use findings describe the late-2024/early-2025 survey period; most anticipated effects have no deadline, while the AI-familiarity forecast explicitly concerns the next five years.
pts.d: The March 2025 publication reports a survey conducted from November 6, 2024, through January 13, 2025 and compares adoption with the 2024 survey. Frequent users are defined as using generative AI at least three times per week; infrequent users use it twice weekly or less. Work-ease percentages apply to current users, whereas most expectations about industry effects cover all respondents, including nonusers. The report notes that 4% of respondents who initially indicated current use subsequently reported never using AI at work; consequently, its 54% adoption figure and its 48% never/nonuser grouping reflect different question-based classifications. Future-use intentions do not specify a date or establish that planned adoption will occur. More than 20% plan use for nearly every listed purpose except patent drafting, but substantial resistance remains: 55% have no plans for contract review and analysis, 72% for client intake and 85% for patent drafting. Even among intellectual-property lawyers, 57% do not plan AI patent drafting. The explicit five-year forecast concerns the importance of familiarity, not a forecast that lawyers will be replaced. The report's text gives 72% overall, 95% of frequent users and 85% of infrequent users for important/very important; displayed rounded chart components differ slightly when summed. Consolidation is only a possibility, without a specified date. The statement that only well-resourced firms devote resources to sustained tool use or development is the report's broad concluding characterisation; its tables also show some investment by smaller firms.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The source distinguishes effects on practising lawyers, junior lawyers, firms of different sizes, clients, low-income people and AI vendors.
pts.d: The direct survey population is lawyers at U.S. law firms, not in-house legal departments or the public. Current users report easier work, and frequent users are more positive about adoption: 73% positive versus 38% of infrequent users and 11% of nonusers. Associates are more concerned than partners about fewer billable hours (38% versus 19%) and white-collar job losses (34% versus 13%). Women more often anticipate reduced opportunities for new lawyers to perform basic legal work than men (64% versus 49%). Reduced billable hours concern 43% of midsize-firm respondents, compared with 20% at small firms and 33% at the largest firms. The report defines small firms as 100 or fewer attorneys, midsize firms as 101–600 and the largest firms as more than 600. Basic usage is described as varying little by firm size or title, but organisational support differs substantially. Forty-four percent of largest-firm respondents report AI-focused hiring, while 85% of small-firm respondents say their firms have neither hired nor are hiring for such roles; 43% at the largest firms do not know their firm's hiring status. Small-firm lawyers face greater reliance on external training, and 50% report no AI-related training versus 21% at the largest firms. AI product costs concern 41% at small firms versus 37% at midsize and 31% at the largest firms. Clients are potential recipients of savings but also subjects of confidentiality risks and use without choice or consent. Low-income clients are a separate anticipated access-to-justice beneficiary, selected by 20% overall and 38% of frequent users; these are lawyer expectations, not client-reported outcomes. Providers operate in a market the report describes as fragmented; the report does not claim that ALSPs displace law firms.
